etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English yielden, yelden, ȝelden (“to yield, pay”), from Old English ġieldan (“to pay”), from Proto-West Germanic *geldan, from Proto-Germanic *geldaną (“to pay”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To pay, give in payment; repay, recompense; reward; requite.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English ȝeld, from Old English ġield, from Proto-West Germanic *geld, from Proto-Germanic *geldą (“reward, gift, money”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeldʰ- (“to pay”).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) Payment; tribute.
(agriculture) measurement of the amount of a crop harvested, or animal products such as wool, meat or milk produced, per unit area of land.
(forestry, fishery) the harvestable population growth of an ecosystem.
(chemistry) the amount of product obtained in a chemical reaction.
(engineering, material science) yield strength of a material.
(hydrology) the volume of water escaping from a spring.
(programming) The situation where a thread relinquishes the processor to allow other threads to execute.
A product; the quantity of something produced.
The explosive energy value of a bomb, especially a nuke, usually expressed in tons of TNT equivalent.
(law) The current return as a percentage of the price of a stock or bond.

quote.citation: 2013 July 6, “The rise of smart beta”, in The Economist, volume 408, number 8843, page 68:
quote.text: Investors face a quandary. Cash offers a return of virtually zero in many developed countries; government-bond yields may have risen in recent weeks but they are still unattractive. Equities have suffered two big bear markets since 2000 and are wobbling again. It is hardly surprising that pension funds, insurers and endowments are searching for new sources of return.

definitions.definition: (finance) Profit earned from an investment; return on investment.
